en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions for the Deliverance of the Daughter of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Meritorious Official, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for the Transmission of the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of śrāvakas.

Furthermore, that householder Anāthapiṇḍada possessed great merit; his wife, children, servants, and retinue were numerous and flourishing. He was wealthy, independent, and had accumulated immeasurable riches, being no different from the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

That elder, together with his retinue, was constantly surrounded by them as they played and enjoyed themselves; then, at one time, his wife became pregnant and after nine months gave birth to a girl of exquisite beauty and supreme grace, whose physical features were perfectly complete from head to toe, such that all who beheld her could not help but love her.
When the girl was born, she possessed various auspicious and virtuous marks; for this reason, her father gave her the name Kṣemāvatī (Well-being).

Furthermore, one hundred and sixty yojanas from this city of Śrāvastī, there was a great city named Puṇyavardhana. There lived an elder named Maudgalya, who also possessed great merit and virtue. His wife, children, servants, and retinue were numerous and flourishing; he was wealthy, independent, and had accumulated immeasurable riches, being no different from the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
Now that elder had a young son named Gośṛṅga, who was of exquisite and peerless beauty, so handsome and sublime that all who beheld him could not help but love and delight in him.

However, both that elder and his son were followers of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika) and held deep reverence and faith in them; consequently, they did not know of the existence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is most supreme and most excellent, nor had they ever heard of the World-Honored One’s most sublime Dharma-gates, nor seen his miraculous transformations and extraordinary deeds previously unknown to them.
These various non-Buddhist practitioners dwell scattered in different places: some in the village of Aulikā, some in the great city of Puṇḍravardhana, and some in the great city of Karmārapura.
At that time, there was a certain non-Buddhist practitioner who had previously been in the city of Puṇyavardhana; he came to the young man Gośṛṅga and said to him:
"For what reason do you not yet take a wife?"
Gosṛta replied, “If there is anyone in the world whose physical appearance and beauty equal mine, I shall marry her.
Then the non-Buddhist said:

“Young man, you should know that in the city of Śrāvastī there is a daughter of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada who is of exquisite beauty and peerless grace; all who behold her find delight in her. You should now seek her as your wife.”
Having heard this, Gosṛta was filled with joy; he immediately changed his usual attire for the robes of an outsider and, carrying his alms bowl, went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having arrived, he proceeded to beg for alms with his bowl in hand and reached the gate of the house where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada resided.
At that time, the woman Bhadrā Kāpilānī heard the sound of begging and immediately took food and drink out to offer as alms.
Once the girl had come out, the youth Gopāla beheld her marks and immediately conceived a sense of love and delight.
That virtuous and poisonless woman, through the power of past causes and conditions, also gazed back at him.
However, when the virtuous woman Viṣaghātinī saw that the cowherd’s son bore the marks of an outsider, she immediately smiled and addressed him thus:
“You are one who lacks correct knowledge, a follower of heterodox paths and different teachings; for what reason do you stay here holding an alms bowl to beg for food?”
Having heard these words, the youth Gopaka also smiled and, refusing to take the food, departed from the house and returned to the city of Puṇyavardhana. He said to his parents:
"Parents, you should know that in Śrāvastī there is a daughter of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada named Kalyāṇabhadrikā; I pray that you now seek her as my wife."
At that time, having heard these words, the householder Mūṣila went to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī and informed him of all these circumstances in detail.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Although I have given my consent, I must wait to consult the Buddha, the World-Honored One; if the Buddha permits it, that would be most excellent."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went in person to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he related the aforementioned matter in detail.
The Buddha said: “Householder!

Your daughter should not shave her head and leave the household life; it would be most excellent if you were to permit her to go there. If she reaches the city of Puṇyavardhana, she will be able to perform vast and supreme auspicious deeds for the sake of the Buddha’s work.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, following the Buddha’s instructions, returned to his own residence. He then brought forth various kinds of precious jewels and other items, prepared all necessary requisites, and according to the worldly rites, gave the maiden Suvīrā in marriage to the youth Ghoṭamukha.
Later on, when that householder Mūṣila was providing a meal for various non-Buddhist ascetics within his own home, he said to Kalyāṇāviṣā:
"Young woman!..."
"Please come and rejoice in this act of giving.

When the woman Supradattā, who had previously not known that she was offering food to various non-Buddhist outsiders, heard the householder’s words, she thought they were the Buddha’s disciples—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda, and others—who had arrived here to receive alms. She immediately leaped for joy and went out, only to see those various non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners with hideous appearances like those of crows, wearing tattered and filthy clothes, their bodies foul-smelling and stinking, naked and shameless like hungry ghosts. Upon seeing them, anger arose in her heart, and she stood to one side.
Then the elder said,
"Daughter, why has your mind become despondent?
The girl immediately replied:
"I am not discouraged; however, regarding this sacrificial assembly currently being held by the householder, if one can make offerings to the assembly of noble ones, one shall obtain supreme merit.
But how can one obtain any benefit by making offerings to these various non-Buddhist practitioners who commit sinful deeds?"
Having heard this, the elder was startled and asked:
"Young woman! Is there indeed anyone in the world who is a more supreme guide than this?"
She replied, "Listen well, householder!
In the city of Śrāvastī there is a great park created by my father, where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, currently resides."

The World-Honored Buddha is the most supreme and most excellent; he is my teacher. His parents are pure, his lineage is noble and eminent, and his clan is Kṣatriya, of the lineage of the Golden-Wheel Kings.

Having renounced the throne of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and cultivate the Way, he grew weary of worldly matters such as wealth and honor. Having practiced all manner of deeds, he subdued Māra beneath the Bodhi tree and attained Buddhahood. His faculties and marks of physical excellence are perfectly complete and majestic; he manifests the appearance of a youth, peerlessly sublime and wondrous. He sports with supernatural powers with unimpeded mastery, his face adorned by the circle of joy, acting in perfect harmony in all places.

Furthermore, he was fully endowed with each of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics. All parts of his body were complete, and his halo shone everywhere; from the crown of his head issued a radiance like a thousand suns, vast, blazing, most excellently adorned, universally virtuous, and as majestic and immovable as a mountain of jewels appearing before the eyes. All sentient beings who beheld him felt love and joy; gazing upon the Buddha’s marks with a devoted heart, they could never tire of doing so.

For the sake of the śrāvakas, he preaches the Dharma according to their needs, analyzing each point individually: this is a causal condition and this is not a causal condition; this is the path of deliverance and this is not the path of deliverance; this is what should be practiced and this is what should not be practiced; this is a matter of supernormal powers and this is not a matter of supernormal powers; this is worldly wisdom and this is the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, whatever the Blessed One has skillfully taught through his expedient means, he has encompassed all other speech with the most sublime Dharma-language; everything he says is solely for the benefit of others. "This is wholesome or unwholesome karma," the Blessed One declares according to reality; "This is the practice to be performed," the Blessed One declares according to reality; "This was said previously, and this was said later," the Blessed One distinguishes each one according to reality.

When the Buddha preached the Dharma, his countenance was serene and joyful; he was far removed from frowning and constantly uttered words that were gentle, compliant, sweet, lovely, skillful, and consoling. Employing various skillful means, he taught the Dharma according to what was appropriate, out of compassion for all sentient beings, seeking their benefit and happiness, so that all sentient beings might be fully tamed.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One distinguished for each of the śrāvakas the dharmas of the noble ones from the dharmas of other paths, and the dharmas that transcend the dust from the dharmas that are peerless, so that the śrāvakas might practice accordingly and in accordance with the truth, attaining perfection in morality, perfection in concentration, perfection in wisdom, perfection in liberation, and perfection in the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Furthermore, wherever the World-Honored One went—to all villages and regions—whether walking or staying, he could not be harmed by any humans or non-humans. At all times, he constantly perceived various forms and signs with his divine eye, constantly heard various sounds with his divine ear, and the light of his wisdom shone forth in vast brilliance; whether it was the proper time or not, he always remained securely established in right mindfulness.
"You should know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such merits; he is called the Supreme Guide of the World.

At that time, among the assembly of non-Buddhist practitioners gathered at the house of the elder Mūṣila, there were those whose roots of goodness had matured. Upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, their hair stood on end and they wept with tears of sorrow. They conceived a pure mind toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and gave rise to deep reverence and faith, immediately saying:
"We vow to go forth as monastics under the Buddha."
At that time, the householder Muśīla, having heard the girl Kalyāṇamitrī describe the virtues of the Buddha, conceived pure faith in the Blessed One and said to the young woman:
"Is it possible for you to enable me to see the Blessed One?"
She replied, "If you wish to see the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, and the noble assembly, you should immediately prepare the most excellent food and drink to offer as an act of worship."
At that time, the elder spoke to his wife, instructing her to prepare food and drink; the wife then replied, "Excellent, Elder!
The food and drink are already prepared."
The elder said to the young maiden, "I do not understand the Dharma; you should invite the Buddha.

Thereupon, the maiden Bhadramatī immediately fashioned a maṇḍala with exquisite flowers toward the direction where the Blessed One resided. From afar, she extended her prostrations, burned various famous incenses, scattered many wonderful flowers, and with single-minded devotion joined her palms to invite the Blessed One, speaking these words:

“The Buddha is the All-Knowing One endowed with great compassion; he causes all sentient beings to see him according to their inclinations and brings them all their desires to fulfillment. Now, this householder Maudgalyāyana, together with his retinue, has conceived a pure heart and desires to see the World-Honored One. Within his own residence, he has prepared various kinds of superior food and drink, wishing to extend an offering. I now invite the Teacher of the World and the assembly of noble ones. I pray that the World-Honored One, out of vast compassion for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, will graciously accept this invitation and come to the householder’s home.”

At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the exquisite flowers scattered by the young girl descended slowly from the sky like a king of geese, arriving before the World-Honored One in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park at Śrāvastī. Their fragrance was like clouds, most supreme and subtle, forming a pavilion that hovered and turned in mid-air.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having seen this omen, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From what direction does this manifested auspicious sign come? Is it a sign that some have come to invite the Buddha?"
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

You should know that one hundred and sixty yojanas from this city of Śrāvastī, there is a great city named Puṇyavardhana. There dwells an elder named Maudgalyāyana, and at present, various non-Buddhist practitioners have gathered within that city.”

"The householder Mūṣila has invited the Buddha and the assembly of śrāvakas; we should go there, each manifesting supernatural transformations to inspire pure faith in those non-Buddhists, and ensuring that those who have already developed faith do not regress. We shall bring about great benefit and happiness for them; this is the sign that he has come to invite the Buddha."

"You should now strike that *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) to assemble the community of bhikṣus and inform them of the time; each of you should manifest supernatural powers and proceed to receive the offerings.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s command, immediately struck the *ghanṭā* to assemble the community of bhikṣus and addressed them as follows:

"Venerable Arhats who have attained supernatural powers, listen attentively to the Buddha’s command: he instructs all the bhikṣus to take note of the time, each manifesting supernatural powers to go to the city of Puṇyavatī to receive the offerings of the householder Mūṣila."

Furthermore, there are various non-Buddhist practitioners currently assembled in that city; I shall cause them to give rise to pure faith, and for those who have already given rise to faith, I shall ensure they do not regress, thereby bringing about great benefit and happiness.
After the Venerable Ānanda had spoken thus, the voting sticks were then distributed, and each of the Arhats received one.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kuṇḍopadhānīya who was the senior elder among the assembly; although he had already realized the fruit of Srotāpanna, he had not yet attained full mastery of the supernatural powers, yet he too received a voting stick.
Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke these words: "Elder Bhikṣus!
This city of Śrāvastī is one hundred and sixty yojanas from that city of Puṇyavardhana; the Buddha has commanded each of you to manifest various supernatural transformations in order to go there."

When the elder bhikṣu heard these words, he immediately cast aside the tally-stick he had previously received. Abiding in accordance with reality through a pure mind, he attained the fruit of arhatship in a single kṣaṇa. He then took up his tally-stick and manifested the six supernormal powers; like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, he leapt into the air and spoke this verse:
"One does not take physical form as supreme, nor does one hold power to be of weight.
Only that which is free from dust and pure is truly adorned; having attained the six supernormal powers, they are all fully complete."

Then, when that day had passed and the dawn of the following morning arrived, the Arhats each manifested various supernatural transformations according to their respective capacities and proceeded in succession to the house of the elder Maudgalyāyana in the city of Puṇyavardhana.

At that time, the householder Mṛṣila, together with his wife and retinue, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground and prepared a most excellently adorned seat. Having set out various kinds of superior food and drink and completed these preparations, the householder and his wife emerged from their home and stood by the gate, waiting for the Buddha’s arrival alongside the maiden Bhadrā Aghatī and the youth Gopaka.
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"Has the Buddha come here to receive my offerings,
or has he gone to another region to receive them?"
Having reflected thus, he stood gazing toward the direction where the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, was located.

At that time, the Venerable Ajñātakauṇḍinya, by means of his own supernatural power, manifested a great chariot drawn by serpents and took his place upon it; he further manifested a fine rain falling gently, with thunder, lightning, and radiant light flashing forth in alternation. Displaying these supernormal powers, he circumambulated that city three times and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:

"Is he who has now arrived riding upon a great serpent-chariot, while a fine rain falls gently from above and the light of thunder and lightning shines forth in mutual reflection—this one who appears with such signs and enters this house—is he your teacher?"
The woman then replied:
"This is not my teacher; he is the World-Honored Buddha’s first disciple to be converted, the foremost of his disciples named Ājñātakauṇḍinya."

When the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, this person was the very first to hear the essentials of the Dharma and attain the realization of its fruit. The Buddha declared that among those who have realized Nirvāṇa, this person is the most supreme and foremost; it is this Venerable One who has arrived here first.

Furthermore, the Venerable Śāriputra transformed a lion-chariot and seated himself upon it; manifesting this supernormal power, he circumambulated that city three times and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has now arrived riding the lion-chariot, manifesting such signs as he enters this house, your teacher?"
The woman then replied, "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Śāriputra.
While this man was in his mother’s womb, his mother naturally possessed sharp and brilliant wisdom, and she was well able to debate and subdue all the teachers of logic within Jambudvīpa."

Once this son was born, his physical appearance was extraordinary, his faculties were well-balanced, and his wisdom was transcendent; his parents, filled with affection and regard for him, immediately summoned various physiognomists to examine the features of the newborn boy.

At that time, the physiognomists were so preoccupied with gazing upon the vast and magnificent physical characteristics of this boy that they forgot to answer the questions regarding his marks posed by the boy’s parents.
At that time, the parents took the boy to a great brahmin and requested him to examine his marks. The brahmin said: "This boy of yours possesses extraordinary physical characteristics;

he shall renounce the world and practice the path within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, exhaust all afflictions, and realize the fruit of Arhatship. Among the assembly of all śrāvaka disciples, he will be able to follow the Tathāgata in turning the wheel of the True Dharma."
If anyone should even briefly behold the face of this youth, that person will immediately attain clear mindfulness and never forget it; how much more so when hearing his spoken words and teachings?
After that brahmin had observed these signs, he later went forth as a renunciant according to those words and realized the fruit.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:

"Even if one were to fill the great ocean with ink, use Mount Sumeru as paper, and take all the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests of the entire earth to serve as pens, and if all the people of the four continents were to spend many eons writing down the vast wisdom of this Venerable Śāriputra, they could never exhaust it."
Furthermore, even if all wise people were gathered together in one place, the wisdom possessed by this Venerable One would still surpass them.

Moreover, it should be understood that, to speak in brief, with the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, all those in the world who possess wisdom do not equal even a sixteenth part of Śāriputra’s vast wisdom when compared to it.
"For this reason, the Buddha declared that among the śrāvakas, this person was foremost in wisdom.
It is this venerable one who has come in due succession.
Thus ends the first fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for the Liberation of the Daughter of Anāthapiṇḍada*, spoken by the Buddha.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions for the Liberation of the Daughter of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.

Furthermore, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa manifested a great golden mountain of dazzling brilliance, surrounded on all sides by various groves of trees and flying birds. Standing upon the summit of this mountain, the Venerable One displayed his supernormal powers; he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has come from the summit of Mount Kanakagiri and now enters this house with such manifestations your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Mahākāśyapa.

Before he left the household life, his family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable quantities of gold, silver, and precious jewels, as well as hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite garments. His retinue was vast and flourishing, and he was revered by all people."
This person, having grown weary of and renounced such matters as wealth and honor, left the household life to cultivate the Way and attained the realization of its fruits.

Furthermore, this Venerable One constantly dwells in one place, always wears a single robe, and possesses few desires while being content; thus, he is able to gather in other sentient beings who are gripped by craving and attachment.
Furthermore, on one occasion, the Buddha shared half of his seat with this venerable one and declared that among those who practice the dhūta austerities, this person is the foremost.
It is this venerable one who has arrived in due order.

Furthermore, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, naturally endowed with marks and signs that were upright, majestic, and extraordinary, manifested a great dragon-chariot upon which he sat; displaying this supernatural power, he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the daughter of the Non-Venomous One:
"Is he who has now arrived riding this great dragon-chariot, manifesting such signs as he enters this house, your teacher?"
The woman replied, "This is not my teacher;
he is a disciple of the Buddha named Mahāmaudgalyāyana. This man possesses great supernormal powers;

once, while on the summit of Mount Sumeru, he subdued the two dragon kings Nanda and Upananda. The palace where Śakra, Lord of Devas, resides is one thousand yojanas in circumference and two and a half yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand jeweled pillars of various kinds. Yet this man, by moving a single toe, was able to cause that entire palace of Śakra to tremble."
Furthermore, on another occasion, the Buddha was staying in the village of Veḷudvīpa and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"At present, there are signs of famine in this village, and it is difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood through begging."

Then, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, without leaving the assembly, immediately turned this great earth and placed it beneath the world-system. He took all the food available in that world-system and established it upon this earth, causing it all to increase. Having performed such deeds in the regions above and below through his supernormal powers, he returned this great earth to its original state, thereby causing all sentient beings to be free from famine.
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana! When this great earth turns, how could all sentient beings possibly find peace and security?”
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

"If I were to hold sentient beings in my left hand and turn the great earth with my right hand, although the great earth would be turned, these sentient beings would remain perfectly secure and at ease, unaware that it was being turned."
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! When it was thus transformed, what thought did you have?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“In my opinion, it would be no more difficult for me to overturn the great earth than it is for a strong man to turn over a plantain leaf.”
The Buddha said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Excellent, excellent!"
"You are able to manifest such supernatural powers and skillful means.
"Householder! The Buddha has declared this person to be foremost in supernatural powers."
"This is the Venerable One arriving in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana manifested a crystal pavilion adorned with various jeweled pillars, nets of many precious gems, and pearl necklaces interspersed and draped about it in vast and magnificent array. Seated cross-legged within the pavilion, he displayed this supernatural power as he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has entered this house—the one who sits cross-legged within this crystal pavilion adorned with various jewels and manifests such signs—is he your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Mahākātyāyana.
He is highly skilled at discerning the words and meanings of the sūtras, and the Buddha has declared him the foremost among those who discourse upon the sūtras."
"This Venerable One is coming here in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila manifested a great ox-cart, seated himself upon it, and displaying this supernatural power, came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has now arrived riding a great ox-cart and manifesting such signs as he enters this house your teacher?"
The woman replied: “This is not my teacher;
he is a disciple of the Buddha named Mahākauṣṭhila. His deportment is dignified and composed, and his faculties are tranquil and subdued.
Since he first left the household life, he has been naturally mature as if he had been ordained for eighty years, and he understands the holy life as if he had practiced it for a long time.”
"The Buddha has declared this person to be foremost among those with few desires;
it is this Venerable One who arrives in due order.

Furthermore, the Venerable Upāli transformed the forest of *kadamba* trees so that they were fully endowed with flowers and fruits of exquisite color. Various exotic birds, such as *kukila* and *śarāra*, gathered upon them, emitting various subtle and lovely sounds. This Venerable One manifested his supernatural power by appearing within the forest; he came from the sky, circumambulated the city three times, and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:
"Is he who has come to this Kadalī grove, manifesting himself within the forest and entering this house with such signs, your teacher?"
The woman immediately replied:
"This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Upāli.

This man is skilled in maintaining the Vinaya practices and his family is of great wealth. Formerly, before he had gone forth, five hundred young Śākya boys, each desiring to leave the household life, adorned their bodies with various jewels. They came before Upāli, each removing the various jeweled ornaments they wore and piling them in one place, and each spoke these words:"
"We have renounced these things to seek the homeless life.
When Upāli saw this sign, he immediately reflected to himself:

"These youths possess such handsome features and noble countenances, and their families are so prosperous; yet they are all able to cast them aside to seek the homeless life. Why is it that I, for my part, take pleasure in finery and ornaments, failing to realize this myself?"

Having reflected thus, on account of these causes and conditions, he likewise renounced his ornaments and other possessions to go forth under the Buddha, becoming the very first to realize the fruit of Arhatship.
"The Buddha declared that this person is foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya;
it is this Venerable One who has arrived in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Aśvajit, his deportment dignified and deliberate and his physical marks serene, came through the air holding his alms-bowl, circumambulated the city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is this person who has come here—whose deportment is composed and deliberate, whose features are serene, and who enters this house carrying an alms-bowl—your teacher?"
The woman immediately replied:
"This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Aśvajit.

Since this man left the household life, his deportment has been dignified and composed, his features serene, and he was able to subdue a drunken elephant to attain the realization of the fruits of the path."
At one time, this person spoke a verse for Śāriputra, saying:
"Because of those afflictions and karma, Which arise and are produced as causes,
Therefore, within this world, They revolve without end."
If the causes of afflictions and karma—these two—are not set in motion, one has transcended the world; this is what the Honored One among Men has taught.
If those two phenomena, birth and old age, do not proceed, [one is liberated].
Therefore, in this world, suffering is definitively non-existent.
He shall attain liberation; this is the supreme, correct speech, which the Great Śramaṇa, the Bull among Men, has proclaimed after having fully realized it.
At that time, as soon as Śāriputra had heard these verses being recited, he immediately understood their meaning and, beneath those words, realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
"The Buddha has declared this venerable one, Aśvajit, to be foremost in dignified deportment;
it is this venerable one who comes in succession.

Furthermore, the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra manifested a golden lotus flower with a thousand petals, each petal as large as a chariot wheel, with a stem of lapis lazuli and filaments of diamond. Thus adorned, its color and light shone brilliantly. Standing upon that lotus, the venerable one displayed this supernormal power: he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has now come from this place—appearing upon a thousand-petaled golden lotus with such radiant splendor and manifesting these signs as he enters this house—is he your teacher?"
The woman then replied:
"This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
This man is skilled at proclaiming the True Dharma; the Buddha has declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma."
"This is the Venerable One approaching in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bahudhānika manifested a great mountain adorned with the four jewels, complete with exquisite banners, pennants, and various jeweled bells; when the wind blew, they chimed harmoniously, bringing joy to all who heard them. While the Venerable One stood upon the mountain peak displaying this supernatural power, he came through the air, circled that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has come from the summit of Mount Ratna and manifested such signs as these, and who has entered this house, your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Bahudhānyaka.

His family is wealthy and prosperous, and all their enjoyments are fully provided. They constantly prepare clean and beautifully adorned couches and seats for the sake of the monastic community traveling from the four directions, supplying whatever they may require."
"The Buddha has declared that among those who enjoy the fruits of merit, this person is foremost in mastery.
It is this venerable one who comes in due succession.

Furthermore, the venerable Aniruddha manifested a golden palace adorned with lapis lazuli and draped with various interlaced jewels, exquisitely beautiful in its ornamentation. Within that palace was a lion throne, and the venerable one sat upon it; manifesting such supernormal powers, he came through the air, circumambulated the city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is he who has now come—the one who sits upon a lion throne in this great golden palace adorned with lapis lazuli, manifesting such signs as he enters this house—is he your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher;
he is a disciple of the Buddha named Aniruddha. In the past, during many kalpas, this man gave rise to a pure mind and offered a single morsel of food to a pratyekabuddha.

By virtue of this root of goodness, he was born seven times as a universal monarch among humans, and again seven times as the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When the remainder of that karma led him to be born into a wealthy family of great means, possessing hundreds of thousands of gold, silver, and precious jewels in vast abundance, he was able to renounce them all to leave the home life and practice the Way."

After going forth, he likewise possessed in full all that was wished for—food, clothing, bedding, and medicine—and having purely cultivated the holy life, he attained the realization of the fruits; furthermore, through causes and conditions, he obtained the pure divine eye.
"The Buddha declared this person to be foremost in the divine eye.
It is this Venerable One who has come here in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable One heard that a multitude of transformed beings were seated upon flower thrones; manifesting such supernormal powers, he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Is the one who has entered this house your teacher, for whom these various flower seats have appeared in such a manner at the place from which he came?"
The woman then replied:
"This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the son of a very wealthy householder.
When this man was born, his parents were filled with joy and said to one another:"
"My household is prosperous and has produced a son of merit; it is fitting that I should extensively bring forth various rare treasures to manifest the signs of our wealth and nobility.
Having deliberated thus, he immediately opened his storehouses and brought out all manner of diverse jewels, summoning all those who were experts in identifying precious gems.
The elder said to them,
"You should determine what the value of these various treasures of mine is. The people replied:
"This treasure is now most excellent and extraordinary; its value is unknown.
The elder then said, "Its price is one koṭi."
The people asked again,
"Is each one of these jewels possessed by the householder worth ten million?
The householder replied:
"So it is, so it is," the people praised, saying,
"The householder's great wealth is without equal."
At that time, the elder spoke these words:
"What name should I give to this son born to me? Someone said:
"When the boy was born, it was heard that there were precious jewels worth ten million [koti].
The elder, acting according to these words, then gave his son the name Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa."
"The Buddha has declared this man to be foremost among those who have transcended the dust of passion.
It is this Venerable One who has arrived here in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Jyotiṣka manifested a peacock chariot and took his seat upon it; displaying such supernormal powers, he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:
"Is he who has now arrived, riding in a peacock-drawn chariot and manifesting such signs as he enters this house, your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Jyotiṣka.

Before he went forth from the household life, he was a wealthy householder in Rājagṛha. Even while manifesting among humans, he enjoyed the superior blessings of the devas; in his own home, he constantly used a cloth made of the finest, most exquisite fine cotton as a pure towel."
Then, at one time, he took a clean cloth and spread it out to dry in the sun; suddenly, a great wind blew it away until it landed before the palace of King Bimbisāra.
When King Bimbisāra saw this clean cloth suddenly lying before him, he asked his attendants:
"This soft, exquisite, and fine cotton cloth is peerless in the world; though I have occupied the royal throne, I have never seen its like. From where has it come? Do you know?"
The attendant minister addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know that in this city there is a wealthy householder named Jyotiṣka, whom the Buddha has declared to be one who currently enjoys celestial blessings among human beings."
"We, your servants, believe these belong to that householder. Your Majesty should summon him for questioning, and he will surely reveal the truth.

At that time, the king immediately summoned the householder to his presence and questioned him in succession regarding the matter. Jyotiṣka said, "This fine cotton cloth was a clean towel used in my household;
it was recently being dried in the sun when the wind blew it here. This is the reality of the matter; I pray that Your Majesty will pardon me."
The king said, "I do not see any fault in you; however, I have heard that you are receiving supreme heavenly blessings—is this indeed true? Jyotiṣka replied:
"So it is, so it is," the King said. "Jyotiṣka!"
"I wish to go to your residence for a brief visit.
Jotika replied, "Great King!"
"I am a subject of Your Majesty and am governed by you; if you would condescend to visit my humble home, I would be deeply honored and delighted.
The King said, "You may return first to prepare food and drink; I shall arrive later."
Jyotiṣka said, "If one is to receive such supreme celestial blessings, there is no need to labor over preparing food and drink; it shall be provided spontaneously.
May Your Majesty proceed now. Thereupon, King Bimbisāra, surrounded by his ministers and retinue, went out to the house of the elder Jyotiṣka, who walked ahead to guide the king.

When the king arrived at the gate of the elder’s house, he saw a female gatekeeper whose physical appearance was dignified and beautiful, adorned with exquisite jewels; the king thought she was the elder’s wife, so he paused for a moment and did not proceed further.
Jyotiṣka said: "Great King!
For what reason do you remain here and not proceed?"
The king said, "Jyotiṣka! Your wife is here;
that is why I am staying for a short while."
Jyotiṣka said, "This is not my wife;
she is a maidservant guarding the gate.
The king then proceeded gradually until he reached the outside of the middle gate, where he saw the same sight as before and again paused for a moment. Jyotiṣka said:
"Why does Your Majesty stop and not proceed?
At that time, the Great King answered as before, and Jyotiṣka said, "This is not the wife of your minister;
she is also a maidservant guarding the gate."

The king then entered through that middle gate and saw a ground of mani-jewels, its brilliance so clear and penetrating that it bore the forms of insects, fish, and other creatures; the king thought it was a pond and paused for a moment, not yet daring to proceed.
Jyotiṣka said, "Great King!..."
"Why do you not proceed further?
The king replied,
"Because there is water here, I do not advance."
Jyotiṣka said, "This is not water; it is ground composed of maṇi jewels.
The king spoke again, saying:
"If this is a ground of jewels, why are there various insects and fish within it?
Jyotiṣka replied, "These are not actual insects and fish; they appear so because they are reflected by the light of the maṇi jewels."

At that time, although the Great King had heard this explanation, he still did not believe it; he immediately took a finger-ring from his own hand and cast it upon the ground. Only when the ring struck the ground with a sound did he finally believe that it was a ground of maṇi jewels.

Then King Bimbisāra entered the house and took his place upon the lion throne; the elder Jyotiṣka stood in attendance at one side. At that moment, the elder’s wife came forward before the king, prostrated herself in salutation, and suddenly shed tears as she withdrew to stand at one side.
The King said,
"Householder! Why does your wife shed tears upon seeing the King?"
Jyotiṣka said: "When the wife of a minor official is permitted to prostrate before the King, her heart is filled with great joy; how could she dare to shed tears?
It is only because the garment worn by Your Majesty has the scent of wood-smoke, and as the smoke stings my eyes, I did not realize that tears were falling."
"Therefore, Great King!
For one who enjoys such superior celestial blessings, the food and drink they desire do not require fire; there are wish-fulfilling jewels that can produce them spontaneously.
The king said:
"Excellent! This matter is rare indeed.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having finished his meal at the house of the elder Jyotiṣka, remained in that house, so captivated by gazing upon it that he forgot to return to the royal palace.
At that time, all the close ministers thought to themselves:
"Has our King not been here for a long time?
If he does not return to the palace, we fear there will be neglect in the affairs of state."
Having had this thought, they both addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
You have remained here for no small length of time; we pray that you return to the palace at once, lest there be neglect in the affairs of state."
The king said to his ministers,
"I have resided here for only a single day, and the affairs of state have not yet been neglected for long.
Then the elder Jyotiṣka addressed the king, saying:
"The King has already stayed in this small cottage for seven days.
At that time, the Great King said to the elder:
"I have indeed stayed in your house for seven days; is this fact not true?"
"Is this fact truly so? Jyotiṣka replied,
"It is indeed so, Great King!"
"It is truly so, Great King!
How would Your Servant dare to speak falsely before You?
The King asked again:
"What signs do you observe within this house to know whether it is day or night?
Jotika replied, "There are flowers that open and close to distinguish between day and night."
There are times when the radiance of the maṇi jewels is intense and times when it is not, by which day and night are distinguished;
there are times when various exotic birds naturally sing together and times when they do not, by which day and night are distinguished.
"Great King, you should know this: when the flowers bloom, one knows it is day; when the flowers close, one knows it is night.
When the radiance of the maṇi jewels is blazing, one knows it is day; when the radiance of the maṇi jewels is not blazing, one knows it is night.
When various birds sing together in harmony, one knows it is day; when they are silent and still, one knows it is night."
"Great King!
I divide day and night by means of such signs as these.
At that time, King Bimbisāra said to the householder Jyotiṣka:
“Rare, rare indeed!
The Buddha’s words are truthful and free from falsehood. The Buddha said that you would receive supreme celestial blessings among humans; what I have now seen is exactly as he described.”
"Then, after King Bimbisāra had spoken these words, he departed from the householder's residence and returned to the royal palace.
Householder Mūṣila!"

Therefore, you should know that this person possesses such superior merit among gods and humans that he was able to renounce all worldly ties, leave the home life to cultivate the Way, and realize the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha declared that this person receives the most supreme heavenly blessings and is foremost among them;
it is this Venerable One who has arrived in due succession.
