Translated by the Dharma Master Śīladharma, recipient of the purple robe and subject, by imperial decree. Furthermore, the Venerable One Hundred-and-Two-Billion-Auditors manifested various colored trees of flowers and fruits, dense and filling the sky; then, manifesting his body within that forest, he exercised this supernatural power and came from the sky, circumambulating that city three times, before descending from the air and entering the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Viśākhā:
"Are those who have come here—the various trees bearing flowers and fruits, and those who manifest such signs within the grove and enter this house—are they your teachers?"
The woman immediately replied, "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.

From the moment this man was born, his feet did not touch the ground, remaining four finger-widths above it. Beneath his feet there were golden hairs as a mark of his extraordinary signs; whenever his feet touched the earth, the ground would shake in six ways."
The Buddha once said to the bhikṣus:

"You should know that this youth Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa has borne this very name throughout ninety-one kalpas; wherever he was born, his feet did not touch the ground. Because he gave rise to a mind of diligent effort regarding the profound Dharma, his meritorious retribution is inexhaustible."
“The Buddha declared that this man was foremost in diligence;
it is this Venerable One who has arrived in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Pindola Bharadvāja manifested a great goose-chariot through his supernormal powers and came from the sky, circling that city three times, before descending from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:
"Is he who has now arrived, riding in a great goose-chariot and manifesting such signs as these, and who has entered this house, your teacher?"
The woman immediately replied, "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Pilindavatsa.
He constantly cultivates the practice of compassion, and the Buddha has declared that this man is foremost in compassionate conduct."
"It is this venerable one who has come in succession.

Furthermore, the venerable Udāyin manifested the supernatural power of transforming a great horse-drawn carriage adorned with the four precious gems; appearing thus from the sky, he circumambulated that city three times and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:
"Is he who has now arrived in this great horse-chariot adorned with the four jewels, manifesting such signs as he enters this house, your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher;
he is a disciple of the Buddha named Udāyin. This man belongs to the kinsmen of the Śākya clan.

Among the Śākyas are King Śuddhodana, King Śuklodana, King Droṇodana, and King Amṛtodana, along with Viśākhā, Ambapālī, Mṛgajā, and others—sixty thousand palace ladies and maidservants as their retinue. These kinsmen possess vast, flourishing, and sovereign wealth and happiness; yet this man renounced them all to leave the household life, practice the Way, and attain the realization of the fruits."
"The Buddha has declared that among the Śākyas, this person is foremost in physical beauty.
It is this venerable one who is coming in due order.

Furthermore, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa transformed a śibikā into the adornment of the four jewels; the venerable one mounted that śibikā and, manifesting this supernatural power, came through the air, circumambulated the city three times, and then descended from the air into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:
"Is he who has now come riding in this vimāna adorned with the four jewels, manifesting such signs as he enters this house, your teacher?"
The woman replied: "This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Mahākapphina.

Having renounced his family and left the household life to practice the Way, he has attained the realization of the fruits [of the path]. He always speaks gentle words and is beloved by all; the Buddha has declared him the foremost among those who speak with gentleness."
"This Venerable One has come here in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Nanda transformed a great grove so that its flowers and fruits were lush and abundant; within it gathered various exotic birds such as geese, swans, parrots, peacocks, śārikas, rucikas, and jīvañjīvakas. Therein, the Venerable One manifested such a form and came through the air, circling that city three times, and then descended from the sky into the house of the elder.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:

"Is he who has entered this house—the one for whom this great grove from which we have come now displays such signs as the flourishing flowers and fruits and the gathering of exotic birds—your teacher?"
The woman immediately replied:

"This is not my teacher; he is a disciple of the Buddha named Nanda, the son of King Śuddhodana and the Buddha’s own younger brother. He is four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha in stature and is fully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man."

In the past, with a pure mind, this person once offered a single parasol—adorned with various jewels, supreme and most exquisite—to the stūpa of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa. By virtue of these causes and conditions, he experienced the ripening of superior merit, becoming a wheel-turning monarch for fifteen hundred lifetimes. Having enjoyed that superior merit, he did not leave the household life; yet, continuing until now, he has left the household life to practice the Way and attained the realization of the fruit. This person, within his dignified deportment, secretly guards all his sense faculties.
The Buddha declared this person to be foremost in the secret guarding of the sense faculties;
it is this venerable one who has come here in succession.

Furthermore, the Venerable Rāhula manifested as a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), his merit, majesty, and appearance being supremely sublime and extraordinary. He was accompanied by a retinue and guards complete with the seven treasures, including eighty-four *koṭis* of brave infantrymen such as the Upasatas; eighty-four thousand elite elephant troops such as the Varāhakas; eighty-four thousand well-trained cavalry such as the Nandyūṣas; and eighty-four thousand chariot troops of exquisite jewels. Furthermore, he was surrounded on all sides by countless hundreds of thousands of attendants, who played hundreds of thousands of kinds of subtle and wonderful music. Adorned with precious banners and streamers leading and following him, a great white parasol covered the crown of the Wheel-Turning King’s head. Displaying this supernatural power, he came through the air, circumambulated that city three times, and remained suspended in mid-air without entering the palace.
At that time, having seen these signs, the elder asked the girl Bhadrottamā:

"Is this Universal Monarch who has arrived—whose merit, majesty, and appearance are so supremely wonderful and extraordinary, and who is accompanied by the fourfold army of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, manifesting such a magnificent sign while dwelling in mid-air—is he your teacher?"
The woman replied, “This is not my teacher;
he is a disciple of the Buddha named Rāhula. This man is the son of the Buddha;

having left the household life to study the precepts, he has attained the realization of the fruits [of the path]. The Buddha declared that among those who train in the precepts, this man is foremost.”
"This Venerable One has successively manifested in the form of a Wheel-Turning King and has come here.
At that time, Rāhula, remaining in the air in the manifested body of a Wheel-Turning King, spoke these verses:
"The Wheel-Turning King's body now manifested by me Is such through the power of supernormal faculties."
As the dragon possesses great power, so do I; I am fully endowed with the seven treasures and the fourfold army.
This manifested body is not real; it is through the skillful means of supernatural powers that I appear according to what is appropriate.
Householder, you should know this as it truly is: I am the Buddha’s son, Rāhula.
Having already attained the fruits of realization and perfected supernatural powers, you are honored by humans and devas and are the refuge for all;
it is by the Buddha’s command that I have come now, and the Great Master Muni shall arrive hereafter.
Having spoken these verses, he descended from the sky and entered the house of the elder.

In this manner, the assembly of great bhikṣus possessing supernormal powers, all acting in accordance with the Buddha’s command, each manifested their own supernatural feats and entered the elder’s house in succession, awaiting the arrival of the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hour had arrived, immediately entered *samādhi* and observed all-pervasively. Emerging from this *samādhi*, his entire body manifested various wondrous colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—as pure, radiant light. Such colored light shone forth extensively, pervading the city of Śrāvastī and reaching as far as the city of Puṇyavardhana. All the people within those cities who were touched by this light, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, beheld the Buddha’s body; it was transparently luminous from within and without, entirely unobstructed.
When the Buddha emitted light, the earth shook violently.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One donned his saṃghāṭī robe and, surrounded by the entire assembly of bhikṣus who were to follow him, including Kuṇḍopadhānīya and others, departed from Śrāvastī and proceeded toward Puṇḍravardhana.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having learned of this matter, immediately came with the host of devaputras from the Form Realm to attend upon the Buddha on his right side as they proceeded;
Śakra, Lord of Devas, having also learned of this matter, immediately came with the host of devaputras from the Desire Realm to attend upon the Buddha on his left side as they proceeded.
Furthermore, five hundred gandharva kings, such as Priyarūpa and others, played hundreds of thousands of kinds of subtle and wondrous music to lead the way before the Buddha;
there were also countless hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, humans, and non-humans following behind the Buddha.

Additionally, innumerable celestial maidens in the void each held *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, celestial *māndārava*, and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, while raining down various exquisite fragrances—such as sandalwood incense, powdered incense, *nigaru* incense, *tagaru* incense, and *tamāla* incense—to make offerings to the Buddha. They also performed the sublime celestial music of those heavens. Thus, this great assembly of devas and humans surrounded [the Buddha] as they proceeded.

At that time, along the way, within a vast wilderness, seven thousand *ṛṣis* who had previously been residing there beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. His perfect radiance shone brilliantly like a thousand suns; he was as majestic and towering as a mountain of jewels appearing, his auspicious and supreme features having no equal, and he was further enveloped by a subtle, golden light that blazed everywhere.
Having seen him thus, they all approached the Buddha, prostrated their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Because these sages had all planted roots of merit in previous lives, they were able to be the very first to behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the seven thousand sages and saw that their roots of merit had matured; he then, within the wilderness, briefly expounded for them the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths according to what was appropriate.

When the rishis had heard this Dharma, their wisdom became firm and their minds were opened and liberated; each was filled with joy. Immediately, they leaped into the air to a height of twenty mountain peaks and together realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Having descended from the sky, they surrounded the World-Honored One and followed him as his attendants.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had delivered these seven thousand sages, he proceeded forward and was about to reach the gate of the city of Puṇyavardhana. He then thought to himself:

"This city of Puṇyavardhana has eighteen gates. If I were now to enter through the western gate, the multitudes at the other gates would not be able to see me. It would be fitting for me now to manifest the body of a Buddha at each of those gates and enter through them, so that all people may see the Buddha’s body, while I myself truly enter through the western gate."

At that time, having formed this thought, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his body and entered through each of the gates, with assemblies of devas and humans surrounding him on every side.

When the Buddha entered the city gate, by means of his supernormal powers, thorns and gravel were naturally cleared away; all impurities were made completely pure, and both inside and out the ground was fragrant and clean, level as the palm of a hand, without any unevenness.

In all the various gateways through which the Buddha passed, those that were low and small naturally became high and large; those places that were narrow naturally became wide and spacious; and among all the elephants, horses, and other creatures within the city, those whose natures were fierce and untamed naturally became tamed.

Furthermore, all the people within the city each looked up at the World-Honored One with great joy. Moreover, by the power of the Buddha’s supernormal abilities, those who were blind were able to see, those who were deaf were able to hear, and those who were mute were able to speak; even those whose faculties were incomplete all became fully restored. Those whose minds were deluded, intoxicated, or deranged all attained clarity and right concentration without distraction. Those who had been struck by poison were entirely freed from it. Those who harbored mutual resentment and hatred turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness. Those who were pregnant gave birth in safety to sons of merit and virtue. And those who were impoverished naturally obtained abundant wealth and treasures.
When the Buddha entered the city, there were such rare and marvelous occurrences that all the people obtained benefit; yet, the Buddha actually entered through the western gate.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had entered the city, he withdrew his emanated bodies until only his single true body remained, and proceeded to the house of the elder Mūśīla.
Then, the woman Bhadrā Viṣapramardinī said to the elder:
"The one who has come here is my Great Teacher, known as the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, the elder and his retinue, beholding the Buddha’s such supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and various marks and signs of excellence, gave rise to a heart of reverent faith and each bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet in salutation.
At that time, the woman Bhadrā Viṣamā, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, leaped for joy and, prostrating with her head at his feet, joined her palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
“My Buddha always speaks the most supreme words, Which are able to subdue the speech of others;
Those who hear them can give rise to a pure mind— I do not see my Buddha in deep suffering.”
Out of compassion, the Buddha has come here; today we have attained great benefit.
With a pure and sincere heart, I prostrate at the auspicious feet of the Tathāgata.

When the woman Bhadrā Aghatā had finished speaking these verses, she took sandalwood water from ox-head sandalwood and offered it to the Buddha to wash his feet. After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat upon the most excellently adorned precious throne; the assembly of bhikṣus also each washed their feet and sat down in order.

At that time, the woman Suvimalā took pure and exquisite food and drink and personally offered it with her own hands to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bhikṣus. The elder and his retinue likewise each took food and offered it to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus. When the distribution of food had proceeded in this manner until all had been served, the Buddha and the bhikṣus ate according to their needs.

At that time, all the brahmins, elders, householders, and followers of non-Buddhist sects such as the Nirgranthas within the city of Puṇyavardhana—countless hundreds of thousands of people—went together to the elder’s house, desiring to behold the World-Honored One.
They thought to themselves:
"The householder’s residence is extremely cramped and cannot accommodate such a multitude of people.
Thus, they all conceived the notion of an obstacle.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, immediately transformed the elder’s house into a crystal palace, transparent and radiant both inside and out, vast and majestic, so that the multitude could each behold the Buddha without any obstruction.
When these multitudes of people had each seen the Buddha, their hearts were filled with great joy; in one voice, they spoke this verse:
"This house of the elder is now composed of crystal, With mani-jewels and pure gold, In which all manner of treasures are reflected."
Pure and vast once more, like the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, each beholds the World-Honored One; this is truly most rare.
We, the entire assembly, gaze upon him as we stand before the Buddha.
All gave rise to pure hearts, reverently joining their palms in salutation.
The Muni dwells amidst the assembly like the moon appearing among the stars;
adorned with all virtues, I therefore take refuge in him.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal and the assembly of bhikṣus had likewise each finished eating, the World-Honored One did not rise from his seat. He remained there, surrounded on all sides by countless hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as other brahmins, elders, householders, tīrthikas, and nirgranthas, including the woman Sunakṣatrā and the elder Mūṣila with their wives, children, and retinues—all of whom sat in attendance listening to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded for the great assembly the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—in accordance with their needs.

While the Buddha was preaching this Dharma-gate, among the non-Buddhists there were those whose roots of goodness had matured; hearing the Dharma, they rejoiced, gave rise to pure faith, took refuge in the World-Honored One, and each obtained benefit according to their respective capacities.

Furthermore, among the assembly, there were those who attained the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), those who attained the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan), those who attained the stage of "Patience" (kṣānti), those who attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, those who attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, those who attained the fruit of Anāgāmin, and those who attained the fruit of Arhat.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the householder Mṛgaśīla gave rise to a pure mind and attained benefit according to his capacity; the woman Suvīrā, through the power of her past roots of goodness and by hearing the teaching of the Dharma, attained the fruit of a srotāpanna.
At that time, all the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How excellent and rare this is!"
This virtuous woman, Untainted, is truly a spiritual friend; because of her, many people have obtained benefit, and she is thus able to perform such Buddha-work.
The Buddha said, “O Bhikṣus!

You should know that this woman, Kalyāṇī Viṣaghātī, has not only served as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) within my Dharma to perform the work of a Buddha today; she has already performed the work of a Buddha by guiding others as a spiritual friend within the Buddhadharma of the past. Listen well as I now briefly relate her story.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!..."

In a past age, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At one time, that Buddha was staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, together with a community of bhikṣus. In that country there was a king named Karuṇā; that king possessed great merit and ruled the world with the True Dharma.

The king had a daughter who, upon birth, naturally possessed a golden wreath upon her head; thus she was named Suvarṇamālā. The king cherished her dearly and commanded his queens, concubines, and attendants to nurture, guard, and look after her until she reached adulthood.

By the power of her roots of goodness from past lives, she conceived a deep love and joy for the Buddha’s Dharma. Hearing that the Buddha was at the Deer Park, she immediately set out for the Deer Park accompanied by a retinue of five hundred palace ladies. Upon arrival, she paid homage to the World-Honored One with her head at his feet in utmost sincerity. The Buddha then preached the essential points of the Dharma to her according to her needs. Having heard the Dharma, her mind was filled with pure faith, and she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall constantly offer food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine to the World-Honored One."
Having made this announcement, he acted accordingly and constantly provided for the World-Honored One with the four requisites.
At that time, King Aśoka suddenly experienced ten dreams during a single night:
first, he dreamed that a great elephant was emerging from a window; although its body had passed through, its tail remained obstructed by the frame.
Second, he dreamed that there was a thirsty person with a well following behind him, yet this person would rather endure the thirst than ever take a drink from it.
Third, he dreamed that someone was trading his pearls for flour.
Fourth, he dreamed that someone was trading his sandalwood for ordinary wood.
Fifth, he dreamed that there was a great garden with flowers and fruits in full bloom, which was suddenly blown down and scattered by a violent wind.
Sixth, he dreamed that there were several small elephants driving a great fragrant elephant away as it fled in haste.
Seventh, he dreamed that there was a monkey covered in filth who ran in all directions, defiling other monkeys, until the entire troop avoided him.
Eighth, he dreamed that a single monkey sat in one place while a multitude of monkeys performed an empowerment ceremony for it.
Ninth, he dreamed of a piece of white cotton cloth; eighteen people each seized and snatched away a small portion, yet the cloth was not torn.
Tenth, he dreams that a great multitude of people have gathered in one place, engaging in mutual strife and disputing right and wrong.
These are the ten dreams he has experienced.
Having awakened from sleep, the king reflected thus:
"That I have had this dream is inauspicious; could it not be that my life-span is to be destroyed?
Having formed this thought, when morning dawned, he immediately assembled his ministers to deliberate together upon this dream.

At that time, none of the ministers were able to determine the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the dreams; the king again summoned a brahmin and related the ten dreams in detail, instructing him to investigate their auspicious or inauspicious signs.
The brahmin said:
"Great King, you should know that this dream is inauspicious; I pray that Your Majesty will perform rites to dispel this ill omen.
The king said:
"What is your teaching? the Brahmin asked.

The king replied, "The maiden with the golden garland whom you love is beloved by all the people as well. I pray that Your Majesty will now take this beloved daughter, pierce your body to draw blood that flows like a river, and cut open your belly to take out your intestines to form a city wall. If you perform such a rite, you will be able to destroy those inauspicious omens; if you do not, there will be a loss to Your Majesty's life."
At that time, the king said:
"Even if I were to lose my own life at this moment, I would never harm that woman, Suvarṇamālā.
Having spoken these words, the king entered the inner palace and sat in silence, resting his chin in his hand with an air of displeasure.
At that time, the maiden Suvarṇamālā saw that the king was sitting in silence with an expression of sorrow and anxiety;
she approached the king and said to him, "Father, for what reason do you have an expression of sorrow and anxiety?"
"Reflecting upon what matter do you think? I pray that Your Majesty will explain it now.
At that time, the king related the ten dreams in their entirety, along with the words of the brahmin, to the maiden Suvarṇamālā.
Having heard this, she spoke again to the king, saying:
"Not far from here, in the Deer Park, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa has gathered together with a community of bhikṣus."

I shall now go with the King to him and inquire about the dream from the Buddha; for the Buddha is the All-Knowing One, and he will surely be able to explain the auspicious and inauspicious signs for the King.

Then King Anukampaka, acting according to those words, went with the maiden Suvarṇamālā and his retinue of ministers to the Deer Park where the Blessed One was. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and withdrew to sit to one side; the maiden Suvarṇamālā and the ministers likewise each paid homage to the Buddha and stood to one side.

At that time, there were also various brahmins, elders, and householders present in the Buddha’s assembly. Then, out of compassion for the king and the members of the assembly, the Buddha preached the Dharma to them as was appropriate, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; having done so, the Buddha remained silent.
King Karuṇāmin rose from his seat, stood before the Buddha, and related the ten dreams in their proper order. Having finished speaking, he said again:
"Because of these omens, I fear there may be a loss to my life-span; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will resolve this for me."
The Buddha said: "Great King!
Do not fear, do not fear!"
"Whatever was seen in that dream is not your concern, nor is it a sign of good or evil for the present time; it shall cause no loss to your lifespan.

Great King, you should know that in a future age when the human lifespan is one hundred years, a Buddha will appear in the world named Śākyamuni, endowed with the ten titles. That Buddha will dwell in the world, expounding all dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings. Having performed the Buddha-work as appropriate, he will enter parinirvāṇa. After his parinirvāṇa, regarding the various activities of the bhikṣu-disciples within the legacy of his Dharma—this dream of yours is a precursor to those events, which I shall now explain to you in sequence."

As for the great elephant that appeared in the King’s dream, which emerged from the window but whose tail was obstructed by it: this refers to those—whether Brahmins, elders, householders, men, or women—who, after that Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, renounce their kinfolk within his bequeathed Dharma to go forth and study the Path. Although they have gone forth, their minds still crave fame and profit and worldly affairs, and thus they are unable to attain liberation.

It is as in the king’s dream, where there was a thirsty man followed by a well, yet that man would rather endure his thirst than ever take a drink from it; likewise, among those who follow the Bequeathed Dharma, there will be bhikṣus who preach the Buddha’s sūtras for the sake of brahmins, elders, and householders, but those brahmins and others will give rise to feelings of aversion and rejection, taking no pleasure in hearing or receiving them.

As for the king’s dream of someone trading his pearls for flour, this refers to those disciples among the monks of that period of the declining Dharma who are unable to cultivate the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the path, meditative concentration, and supramundane dharmas according to the Buddha’s authentic scriptures; instead, they take pleasure in cultivating worldly treatises, incantations, songs, and verses.

As for the person in the King’s dream who traded sandalwood for ordinary wood, this refers to those bhikṣus within the Buddha’s bequeathed Dharma who trade the Buddha’s sūtras for worldly secular texts and the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.

As for the king’s dream of small elephants driving the great fragrant elephants away in flight: this signifies that within his legacy-dharma there will be bhikṣus who break the precepts and lack virtue; seeing the assembly of bhikṣus who uphold the precepts and possess virtue, they will skillfully employ expedient means to ostracize them and drive them far away.

As for the king’s dream of a great garden with flowers and fruits in full bloom that was suddenly blown down, scattered, and destroyed by a fierce wind: this signifies that within his legacy, there will be pure bhikṣus who maintain the precepts, possess virtue, and are learned, who dwell in a monastery (saṃghārāma). However, they will be collectively destroyed by a multitude of coarse and evil bhikṣus who have not cultivated their bodies, minds, or wisdom;
having thus destroyed the monastery, they will further cause the most excellent undertakings of the pure bhikṣus to be utterly ruined as well.

The dream of the king in which a monkey covered in excrement ran in all directions, defiling other monkeys so that the entire crowd avoided it, represents those bhikṣus who will break the Dharma left behind by him; having themselves violated the pure precepts and lacking a sense of shame or remorse, they will in turn slander virtuous bhikṣus who uphold the precepts in the presence of kings and ministers of pure faith.

As for the king’s dream of a single monkey sitting in one place while a multitude of monkeys performed an empowerment ceremony for him: this refers to those monks within the legacy of that [degenerate] Dharma who do not cultivate superior practices and lack virtue, yet are collectively established as the leaders of the Saṃgha, presiding over those who possess virtue and cultivate superior practices.

Regarding the king’s dream of a single white cotton cloth from which eighteen people each seized a small portion without the cloth being torn: this signifies that within the *śāsana* left behind by him, various disciples will give rise to divergent views and attachments, thereby dividing the Buddha’s teachings into eighteen schools; yet, even though this occurs, the Buddha’s teachings shall not be destroyed.

As for the king’s dream of a great multitude of people gathered in one place, mutually quarreling and contending over right and wrong: this refers to the various bhikṣus within that period of the bequeathed Dharma who gather to discuss worldly matters such as fame and gain; due to these causes and conditions, they quarrel with one another and fail to attain tranquility, gradually causing the World-Honored One’s pure Dharma to perish.
"Great King!
These ten dreams are none of your concern; they are omens pertaining to another, for which you should not fear. Your life will not be lost; you should set your mind at ease."
At that time, having heard the Buddha explain the matter of his dream, King Karuṇāla was filled with great joy; he prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and returned to his royal palace.

"O Bhikṣus! After that Tathāgata Kāśyapa had finished explaining the king's dream out of compassion for him, he further preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to the assembled multitude. At that time, there were eighty-four thousand people in that assembly who all realized the Truth and attained its benefit."
"O Bhikṣus! What do you think?
Is that woman Suvarṇamālā—who, within that Buddha-dharma, acted as a spiritual friend to King Karuṇā for his sake and established the work of a Buddha—anyone else?"
She is none other than this very woman, Śunandā. Monks!

Therefore, you should know that this Śunandā was already a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) within the Buddha-dharma of the past, and now, within my Dharma as well, she acts as a spiritual friend to many people, causing many to obtain benefit.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions was that woman with the golden wreath born with a natural golden wreath upon her head during the time of that Kāśyapa Buddha?”
"Furthermore, for what reason was he born into a royal family and experienced great wealth and pleasure?
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus!"
In a past life, that woman Suvarṇamālā was a poor woman in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; she traveled about begging for various ornaments and fragrant ointments.
Within a stūpa of a single pratyekabuddha, he adorned and decorated it, giving rise to a pure mind and making this vow:

"By these roots of goodness, may I, in every birth throughout my lives, have a golden wreath upon my head; may I be born into a great wealthy family with sovereign riches and power, and perform the work of a Buddha."

"O Bhikṣus! That poor woman at that time was none other than this Kāñcanamālā, who, through those roots of goodness and the power of her great vow, was born with a natural golden garland upon her head wherever she was reborn throughout five hundred lifetimes."

"O Bhikṣus! Therefore, at this present time, because of her past roots of goodness and the power of her great vows, this virtuous and poisonless woman has been born into the wealthy household of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, where she skillfully guides others and performs the work of a Buddha."
Therefore, one should know that determinate wholesome karma and its determinate wholesome retribution can never be lost at any time or in any place.

Just as the earth element possesses the nature of solidity and not the nature of flowing moisture and so forth belonging to the water, fire, or wind elements, so too it is with the various distinctions of the aggregates, bases, and elements: whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma all sentient beings perform is likewise [inexhaustible].

Because the distinctions among various karmic causes differ, the resulting retributions obtained are not uniform; even if one were to pass through a hundred kalpas, the law of cause and effect remains definitively without fail.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!

For this reason, sons and daughters of good family should engender deep pure faith, respect, and veneration toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they should faithfully believe in, accept, uphold, proclaim, disseminate, and practice according to the principle this sūtra."
“You monks, you too should train yourselves in this way! At that time,

after the Blessed One had related the past causes and conditions concerning the woman Bhadrā Kāpilānī to the monks, he taught the True Dharma as was appropriate for each— just as he had previously done for Bhadrā Kāpilānī and the kinsmen of the householder Mṛṣila, and even for the brahmins, householders, and lay devotees in the city of Puṇyavardhana, as well as for all other assemblies of devas and humans— so that each obtained benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus vanished from the midst of the gathering and traveled to Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove at Śrāvastī, where they reappeared.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder’s retinue, including the woman Sunakṣatrā, the bhikṣus, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for the Liberation of the Daughter of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll II.
